During his three and a half decades in public service, Sam Brownback earned the unusual distinction of being the only American to have served as a U.S. congressman, U.S. senator, state governor, and U.S. ambassador. And it was perhaps in that final role—as ambassador at large for international religious liberty—that Brownback finally found his true calling. For three years, starting in 2018, Brownback worked to strengthen the influence of “religious freedom diplomacy” within the halls of the State Department and the U.S. diplomatic corps. And by many measures, his success was astonishing. At the State Department, Brownback led what he called a “global religious freedom movement.” He convened massive annual religious freedom ministerials in Washington, D.C., attended by high-level government delegations from more than 100 countries along with more than 1,000 leaders of civil society organizations. He was also a key player in forming the International Religious Freedom or Belief Alliance, which now counts 32 countries as members. Since leaving the State Department in 2021, Brownback has continued his role as international religious freedom advocate, although now in a private capacity. He continues to speak and write about religious liberty issues, and he founded the annual International Religious Freedom Summit in Washington, D.C.—now in its sixth year—which draws hundreds of advocates, faith leaders, and government officials from around the world. Brownback’s most recent book, authored with Michael Arkush, is called China’s War on Faith . It takes a deep dive into the Chinese Communist Party’s campaign against religious believers, and what this reveals about the global struggle to protect religious conscience. Liberty editor Bettina Krause, together with Alan Reinach, president of the Church State Council, recently interviewed Ambassador Brownback for their weekly podcast Just Liberty . While the conversation has been edited for length and clarity, you can listen to the entire interview on YouTube at @LibertyMag_1906 or by searching for “Just Liberty” on your podcast platform of choice. Bettina Krause : When you served at the U.S. State Department, you traveled the world, visiting different countries where religious freedom is being violated. So, why, in this new book, are you focusing exclusively on China? Sam Brownback : All roads lead to Beijing. When you’re looking at persecution or the enabling of human rights abuses in many different places, much of this couldn’t happen without a complicit Beijing. The Chinese Communist Party may not be directly operating it, but they’re encouraging it. It’s such a central tenet of Communism that you must control people of faith—of any faith. And the Chinese Communist Party spreads its tentacles into the authoritarian sphere of influence that China has around the world. We’re seeing police states developing within many different authoritarian regimes today, and much of the surveillance technology they’re using was beta tested, developed, and deployed by the Chinese Communist Party. Alan Reinach : What is it about freedom of religious conscience that presents such a challenge for totalitarian governments? Brownback : Totalitarian regimes cannot stand any allegiance that’s higher than the government, period. They say, “Look, we are the decision makers. We are the authority.” They’ve found, over the years, that people of faith will stand up and fight—and, when pushed, they will actually put their faith above even their own lives. That is just such a core challenge to a totalitarian state, and particularly to a Communist state that is officially atheistic. This is why I argue that America’s commitment to religious freedom as a cornerstone human right is a strategic asset—and it’s one that we should be using in this era of global expansion of totalitarian movements. Eighty percent of the world’s people have some kind of faith orientation. So this is a value that’s important to the vast majority of the world’s population. Reinach : Several decades ago a Roman Catholic cardinal in the Philippines, the perhaps inappropriately named Cardinal Sin, was instrumental in leading the opposition against Ferdinand Marcos, which ultimately resulted in the overthrow of Marcos. I’m not a China expert, but if I were sitting in Beijing, I would take a lesson from that. I would become very suspicious of any kind of organized power, such as religion, that can pose an institutional threat to the government. Brownback : This threat is even more specific to Communism. I think, for instance, of the fall of the Soviet Union and the role of Pope John Paul II, who was Polish. He shows up in Poland behind the iron curtain, and says, “Be not afraid,” to a Polish population that’s historically Catholic but hadn’t been to Mass in decades. He says, “Be not afraid,” and the people who were afraid—who were shaking in their boots—were the Communist leaders of Poland. And before long, it was done. It was over. They had lost power. I believe that the Chinese Communists have studied that model and that fall. They’ve studied the Jewish refuseniks and what they did to undermine the authority of the Soviet Union; they’ve studied the evangelicals and what they contributed, as well. Communism seems to have about a 70-year life expectancy in many countries, and the Chinese communists, I think, are trying to extend this. And one of the key groups they need to control is people of faith. Krause : I visited China some 15 years ago now with a group of church leaders, and we met with Chinese Communist Party leaders who were part of the so-called Three-Self Movement, which is kind of the umbrella organization for Protestant Christianity in China. What is it like to be a Christian believer today within the Three-Self Movement? Brownback : This Three-Self Movement in China is a top-down, government-controlled church. Now it is a church, in that there are people within it who do have fundamental beliefs in the Bible and God. But the church structure itself is forced to answer to the government. It cannot ever be critical of the government, and the church leadership must be vetted and controlled by the government. And even the church’s teachings must comply with government demands. During the past several years the Chinese Communist Party has been rewriting and revising portions of the Bible so that it’s more in line with their view of Christianity. This is an officially atheistic organization rewriting Holy Scripture! And more than this, they also believe they have the right to appoint the next dalai lama—the leader of Tibetan Buddhism. This is really about controlling religion and religious expression, and to control folks whose ideas may be more in line with their faith than with their allegiance to the government. Reinach : Most of the stories American Christians hear about persecution or repression in China involve Christians. But there are other faith groups that are suffering as badly or even worse. Is that right? Brownback : Christians don’t have it near as bad as, say, the Falun Gong, which is kind of a blended spiritual movement of Buddhism and Taoism. I often described Falun Gong as the type of spirituality that a grandma in China used to practice—it’s a kind of fusing together of ideas from various Eastern religions, and it wasn’t treated as a problem. But then in the 1990s a guy came along and blended these ideas together officially to create a new religious movement, and it just took off. Within seven years there were some 90 million adherents. Well, the Chinese Communist Party came down like a ton of bricks on the Falun Gong. They even began a program of forced organ harvesting—an attempt to literally try to wipe this movement out. That’s why I say that China is engaged in a genocide against Falun Gong. And of course the Communist leaders also want to control the Tibetan Buddhists. There was one party secretary, Chen Quanguo, who was originally the party chairman over Tibet, and he worked to subdue the Tibetan Buddhists. Well, Chen Quanguo was then moved over to Xinjiang Province to deal with the Muslims there, which were a bigger and more difficult religious population. And in Xinjiang, Chen established a diabolical police state, which included concentration camps housing more than a million people. Even if you weren’t in one of these camps, you were being constantly tracked by cameras and other surveillance technology. This was something that really scared me when I first saw it, because it provides a model for authoritarian regimes elsewhere. Our modern era of technology provides a level of surveillance that these regimes could never have dreamed of a generation ago. Krause : You mentioned earlier “organ harvesting” as one measure the China Communist Party has taken to subdue some religious populations. But this sounds almost unbelievable. When you served as ambassador for international religious freedom, did you have to be “educated” into the realities of religious freedom abuses? And did you ever think, This sounds too horrific to be true? Brownback : I had those questions and doubts for a decade. When I was in the Senate, these Falun Gong practitioners would come up and tell me about these things. And I’d say, “Yeah, I hear you.” And they would give me their evidence, and I would reply, “OK.” But it just sounded so diabolical that I could not believe that people could imagine and implement such a system—something that would make a medieval executioner blush. But I kept talking with people and seeing new data. I interviewed a gentleman who had an organ harvested—part of his liver. I looked at the forensic medical reports. And you have to say, “Yes, it’s happening.” And then in 2020 Sir Geoffrey Nice from Britain led an investigation into what was taking place. They went through the numbers of organs that are harvested and transplants taking place annually in China. And they concluded that you can’t do those numbers of transplants without having some sort of forced system in place. Reinach : I’m almost afraid to ask: What happens to folks when they take the organs? Are they taking enough to kill them? Brownback : In almost all situations, yes. Falun Gong practitioners are given a death sentence on some sort of treason charge, and so their eyes, heart, lungs, liver, kidney, and multiple organs can be harvested. A kind of “organ tourism” developed for a while where you could sign up for a kidney, for instance, and schedule it—show up at a certain place, and they would get you a kidney. They extended this practice within the Chinese Muslim population and then advertised this in the Muslim world as “halal organs” available for transplants. Israel, I believe, was the first country to ban organ tourism to China. And praise God, they did that. I’ve talked with those in the Muslim world, and asked, “Why don’t you guys speak out more about what’s going on in Xinjiang? Because this is a predominantly Muslim population.” And they won’t and they haven’t. They say that the Chinese play rougher than we do. But China is the only country I know of in the world where you cannot legally name a child Muhammad. There are 50 or so majority Muslim countries in the world—why should they follow the lead of a nation that bans the most popular male name in their own country? Shouldn’t that tell you something? I want to say one other thing here. I love China and the Chinese culture. My wife and I adopted a young girl from China 25 years ago, and she’s a wonderful member of our family. This is not about China or its culture. This is about the Chinese Communist Party and a dictatorship that they want to use to run the world. Krause : Ambassador, are there connections between what’s happening in China and what’s happening within other repressive regimes around the world? Brownback : Well, the unfortunate thing is that technology can easily be exported to other countries. And you can use this technology to find a needle in a haystack. You can find the one guy or the one woman out there who’s organizing a Bible study or is leading a worship group. You can do key word searches on these things. There are many different listening and tracking devices that can find the word “Muhammad” or “Lord” or “Allah” or “God” within trillions of names and data points and to pinpoint who that person is. And you can find not only the person who’s originating these conversations but also the network of people they’re talking to. In China they’ve started developing individual “social credit scores”—marking down your social credit if you went to the mosque, for instance. It also affects the people that you then talk with, and they get caught in the same lower social credit score. And this can keep you from getting the housing you want or your child getting into a particular school. Reinach : It strikes me that George Orwell lived and died too soon, because his vision of the totalitarian society doesn’t begin to deal with the reality that we’re seeing today. Brownback : I can’t argue with you on that—but it gets worse. All these electric cars now, particularly coming out of China—these can be watching devices if you’ve got them plugged in and connected right. I don’t know if you saw recently, but there are some electric lawn mowers that have sensing devices in them. I don’t want to see a spy behind every lawn mower, but we need to understand that there’s just too much capacity, combined with too much desire for information and control. Krause : What makes these challenges so resistant to diplomatic efforts? Why haven’t we made more progress on improving human rights in China? Brownback : For a long time many people at the highest levels of our government had a complete disregard for anything religious. They didn’t think religious people were particularly helpful. Many believed that religion, in fact, was a cause for many wars and conflicts, so they thought, Let’s get away from religion! They couldn’t see that most people have a faith orientation, and you have to address that if you’re going to be able to connect with them and their culture. Most cultures are built on a set of religious values, whether that’s the Indian culture built on Hinduism or the Islamic culture in Muslim-majority countries. I think the U.S. just didn’t want to get into that space. But once we started to, it was clear that this approach starts to address a lot of issues. And so you get breakthroughs such as the Abraham Accords, which come out of a theological approach to the underlying issues that people can identify with. They understand, “Well, I’m in the family of Abraham.” You connect with people, and bring them along with you, when you go to the very roots of their beliefs. Reinach : My perception has been that, as a nation, we sometimes emphasize human rights in our foreign policy, to a greater or lesser extent, but the more consistent theme is economic policy or other types of policy interests. That makes advocacy for human rights and religious freedom a tough uphill battle. Is that fair? Brownback : Completely. Until the past 10 to 15 years, that was completely true. It was a useful thing, once in a while, to use human rights as a talking point. But we rarely talked about religious freedom. Then you started hearing people say, particularly in the first Trump administration, “We’re going to make religious freedom a cornerstone human right.” The theory being that if you can get this one thing right, you can then build around that—freedom of assembly, freedom of speech, and other rights. The human right of the soul is the one that’s closest to who you are as a person. And that approach did start gaining some traction. We’re always best when we lead with our values, and religious freedom is a bedrock value—one that happens to go right to the heart of the Chinese Communi

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y.text: Figure caption, Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages By Orla Guerin Senior International Correspondent ,Â Reporting from Aden Published 36 minutes ago From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival. They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces. When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks â the twins protected only by blankets. What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden. "It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused." Image caption, The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden "It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused." As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhaustedâ¦ there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse." By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs. Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured. Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk. The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet. Image caption, More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed. The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer. Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz. The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices. The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes. Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away. Image caption, Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018. "I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself." Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred. "I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]." Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space. Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing." Image caption, Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut. There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment. That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor. "It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says. "We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them." A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line. Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year. Image caption, Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon. "Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again." They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics. "Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital." She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them. Image caption, Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood. As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there. So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.
